title: Two Doors

post.author: u/night_analyst_thandeka
post.title: I count the numbers behind our shop's two chat assistants. Customers preferred the new one, the test said it was sure, and it costs us more every week.

blocks.text: I'm Thandeka, the night analyst at Fernhallow, an online shop for walking boots and coats. An analyst counts what happened; I do it overnight, so the numbers are ready by morning. We rent an old cinema on Brackenbury Street, and my desk sits in the hallway between its twin doors, still marked Screen 1 and Screen 2.

On our website, customers can chat with an assistant before they buy. It is a language model, a program that writes text one likely word at a time. Every chat ends with a question: did this help? Thumbs up or thumbs down, and no tap counts as down. The share of chats that end thumbs up is our thumbs-up rate.

In September, Mr Coxwell, who runs the product, wanted a warmer, more confident assistant. Call it B; the current one is A. To compare them on real customers, we ran an A/B test. Each new visitor was sent to A or B by a computer's coin toss, and kept there on every visit. Two doors, and a coin chose yours.

Before the start, we worked out how many chats each door needed for a fair chance of spotting a rise from 70% to 72%: at least 8,077. That number is called the sample size. At about 600 chats a door a day, it meant 14 days, from a Monday to the Sunday after next.

Every morning the team read a dashboard, a screen of the test's numbers counted from day 1. Beside the two thumbs-up rates it showed a p-value. It answers one question: if the two doors were really the same, how often would a gap this big turn up by luck alone?

When the p-value fell below 0.05, fewer than one time in twenty, the dashboard called the gap significant and turned green. Day 4, a Thursday, was a good day for B. Each line below is one morning: the days it counted, each door's thumbs-up rate so far, and the p-value.

That Friday morning, Mr Coxwell called the test for B. Our changes go live in a release every second Monday, and the next one was day 15, the day after the plan's last day. So the coin kept tossing for all 14 days. Nobody looked at the dashboard again.
The door everyone preferred. A test that said it was sure.

B has served every customer for five weeks. Last week Ms Dabrowska, who runs the refunds desk, asked why refunds were up by half. Tonight, in the hallway, I matched each refund to the chat before it and counted the whole fortnight by door.

B got 72.3% in week 1 and 69.8% in week 2; A got 69.9% and 70.0%. Refunds over the fortnight: A 252 of 8,407 chats, 3.00%; B 378 of 8,393, 4.50%.

blocks.text: B's lead was nearly all in its first week. Its refunds ran half as high again as A's, on every one of the 14 days. Mr Coxwell says the test was significant, and B stays. What do I tell him?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that hallway is haunted, though I'd prop one door open. A thumbs up is the customer telling you how the chat felt; that is called explicit feedback. A refund is the customer showing you, without being asked, how the advice worked out; that is implicit feedback. Both come from the same chats. Two questions. After day 4, what did the dashboard say each morning up to day 14, and how did B do in its second week on its own? And during the test, where could anyone have seen B's refunds, and how long after a chat does a refund arrive?

replies.author: u/night_analyst_thandeka
replies.text: Counting to day 5 it was 0.014, and it stayed green counting to day 10, at 0.049. Counting to day 11 it went to 0.073, and counting to day 14 it ended at 0.116: A 70.0%, B 71.1%, a lead of 1.1 points, not significant. In week 2 alone, B got 69.8% and A 70.0%. Refunds were nowhere on the dashboard. They arrive 2 to 7 days after the chat, and the refunds desk counts them once a week.

comments.author: u/ship_it_gillow
comments.text: p below 0.05 is p below 0.05. On day 4 the result was significant: less than a one-in-twenty chance it was luck. That is the line every lab in the world uses, and B crossed it. What happened after that is the shine wearing off the test, not B getting worse, and 1.1 points is still a lead. Your customers told you with their own thumbs which door they liked. The refunds are a sizing problem. Fix the size charts and keep B.

replies.author: u/night_analyst_thandeka
replies.text: Mr Coxwell has the day 5 screenshot pinned above his desk.

comments.author: u/refunds_desk_dabrowska
comments.text: I run the refunds desk. Since B went to everyone, refunds have run at about 378 a week; under A it was about 252, with the same 1,200 chats a day. Most of the new refund notes quote the assistant: true to size, you'll be fine in a 9, this coat runs warm so go down a size. When A's customers mention the chat at all, they say it asked what size they usually wear. One more thing: a refund only reaches me 2 to 7 days after the chat, and I report them on Mondays.

reply.prompt: Mr Coxwell says the test was significant, B stays, and next month's assistant test will run the same way. What should Thandeka tell him? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Fix the sample size before starting, run to the end, and stop B early only if refunds rise.
options.part2: Mr Coxwell put everyone back on A with the next release, and we wrote the rules for next month's test before it starts: 8,077 chats a door, 14 days, one look at the end. One number may stop B early: its refund rate, with a line at 3.5%, half a point above A's usual 3.00%. To show him, I replayed the logged fortnight under those rules. Day 4's green never counts, because nobody reads it. At the end of day 8, B's first day of refunds is complete: 27 of 602 chats, 4.49%, over the line, and B stops, on a day when its thumbs-up lead was still 2.0 points with p = 0.031. Had it run, day 14 said 1.1 points, p = 0.116: no winner. Ms Dabrowska asked why the line waits a week. Because the refunds do.
options.senior: Decide the sample size, the length and the one decision rule before the first customer walks through a door, then look at the main number once, at the end. Name the numbers that must not get worse, here refunds, with a line that stops a variant early when it is clearly doing harm, and expect them to arrive late. Read the thumbs beside the refunds, and split the result by week to see a novelty effect fade.

options.text: Keep B: its thumbs-up rate was higher, and the test was significant on the day it was called.
options.part2: B stayed. I replayed the logged fortnight for Mr Coxwell anyway. The morning of day 5: p = 0.018, green. Day 14, the day the plan said to decide: a lead of 1.1 points and p = 0.116, not significant. B by week: 72.3%, then 69.8%, below A's 70.0%. Refunds: 4.50% against 3.00%, higher on every day of the fortnight. At 8,400 chats a week, that is 378 refunds a week against 252. He said the new size charts would fix it, and ordered them.
options.senior: A p-value is only as good as the rule it was read under. Read once, at a sample size fixed in advance, below 0.05 means a gap that size turns up by luck in fewer than 1 in 20 tests. Read every morning and acted on at the first green, it means much less. And a significant lead on the thumbs says nothing about refunds, which nobody was measuring.

options.text: Run the test again, checking daily, and stop as soon as either door is clearly ahead.
options.part2: Mr Coxwell liked it: faster answers. Before the rerun, I put the rule through the sim on 200 made-up tests where both doors held A, so any winner was luck. Checking every morning and stopping at the first green, 43 of the 200 found a winner. Checking once, on day 14, 7 of 200. On our own logged fortnight the daily rule stops on day 4 again and picks B again. Mr Coxwell said 43 sounded like a lot of winners. It was a lot of false ones.
options.senior: Each morning's look is another chance for luck to dip below 0.05, so stopping at the first green finds false winners far more often than the 1 in 20 the p-value promises: 43 in 200 here, against 7 in 200 with one look. If you need to look early, plan the looks in advance and use a method built for them, such as a sequential test, with a stricter line at each look.

options.text: Judge the two doors by refunds alone, since money is what really matters to the shop.
options.part2: We dropped the thumbs and judged by refunds. Replayed on the fortnight, it picks A: 3.00% against 4.50%, p below 0.001. But day 14's refunds were only complete on day 21, a week after the test ended, and on the morning of day 5 not one day's refunds was complete. Mr Coxwell asked what it would say about an assistant that talked every customer out of buying. Nothing bad: no sales, no refunds.
options.senior: Refunds are the right thing to protect and a poor thing to steer by alone. They arrive late, they say nothing about whether the chat helped, and a door that sells less refunds less. Keep a main measure, here the thumbs, and make refunds a guard-rail metric: a line that must not be crossed, checked as the refunds arrive.

sim.title: Replay the fortnight behind the two doors
sim.lede: You're Thandeka in the hallway, with the logged fortnight. For each of the 14 days the sim holds each door's chats, thumbs up and refunds, about 600 chats a door a day; nothing is made up except the A/A tests below. Each day's thumbs-up rate and p-value count from day 1. The p-value is worked like this: put both doors together, all thumbs up over all chats, (upA + upB) / (nA + nB), call it r; the standard error is the square root of r x (1 - r) x (1/nA + 1/nB); z is B's rate minus A's, divided by the standard error; and p is the chance of a z at least that far from 0, either way, on the bell-shaped curve that luck follows. Below 0.05 is significant. Every refund is known by the end of the 7th day after its chat, so a refund line can first look at the end of day 8. Stop rule, each day in turn: if the refund line is on and B's known refund rate is over it, B is stopped; else if the team checks every morning and the p-value is below 0.05, the test is called; else on the planned last day the test ends and its p-value decides. The A/A switch runs 200 seeded tests in which both doors hold the same assistant, so any winner is luck: every chat is a thumbs up with chance 70%, on the logged daily counts.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you open as run, checked every morning: the test is called on day 4, A 69.8% against B 72.9%, p = 0.018. Work day 4 by hand under the table. Turn the morning checks off: day 14, lead 1.1 points, p = 0.116, no winner. Read B by week: 72.3%, then 69.8%. Set the refund line at 3.5%: B is stopped on day 8, 27 refunds in 602 chats. Turn the morning checks back on: day 4 ships B before the line can look. Switch to A/A: 43 of 200 false winners checking every morning, 7 of 200 checking once. Then try each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing behind the doors was haunted. The team read a significance test every morning and stopped at its first green, on a good day in B's first week, when the new voice was still new. Nobody was watching the one number that showed B costing the shop money.

steps.title: Two doors and a coin: why the coin decides.
steps.text: An A/B test is a kind of online evaluation: it learns from real customers after a change is live. It runs in four steps. First, a visitor arrives. Second, a computer tosses a coin and sends them through door A or door B. Third, the website remembers the door, so the visitor gets the same assistant on every visit. Fourth, at the end, the two doors' numbers are compared. The coin is the point. If customers chose their door, the curious and the keen would pick the new one, and the two doors would differ in their people as well as their assistants; any gap could be either. Letting chance decide like this is called randomisation. A coin makes the two crowds alike in everything except the door, so a gap in the numbers can be put down to the assistant or to luck, and the p-value measures the luck. What can go wrong: the split drifts from half and half, or one customer sees both doors on two devices.

steps.title: The p-value, worked by hand on day 4.
steps.text: The test Fernhallow's dashboard used compares two shares, in four steps. First, put both doors' chats together: days 1 to 4 had 1,676 thumbs up of 2,400 chats at A and 1,750 of 2,400 at B, so 3,426 of 4,800, 71.4%. Second, the standard error, the size of gap luck alone usually makes: the square root of 0.714 x 0.286 x (1/2,400 + 1/2,400), which is 0.0130. Third, the z-score, how many of those luck-sized steps the gap is: B's rate minus A's, 72.9% minus 69.8%, a gap of 0.0308, divided by 0.0130, is 2.36. Fourth, p: on the bell-shaped curve that luck follows, a score at least 2.36 from zero, either way, turns up 1.8% of the time, so p = 0.018. What it means: if the doors were the same, a gap this big would show by luck in about 1.8% of tests read once. What it is not: the chance that B is not better. And it holds only if the sample size was fixed and the test read once. Day 14, with all the chats, says p = 0.116.

steps.title: Fix the sample size first, and don't stop on a good day.
steps.text: The sample size is set before the start, from three choices: the smallest gap worth catching (70% to 72%), how often you accept a false alarm (5%), and how often you accept missing a real gap (20%, so an 80% chance of catching it, called power). The usual formula gives 8,077 chats a door: 14 days here. Then the test runs to the end and is read once. Reading it every morning and stopping at the first p below 0.05 gives luck 14 chances instead of one. Evan Miller showed this in 2010: peek ten times and what looks like 1% significance is really 5%. The sim checks it on 200 A/A tests, where both doors hold the same assistant and every winner is false: checked every morning, 43 of 200 found a winner; checked once on day 14, 7 of 200. Fernhallow's green on the morning of day 5 was one of those mornings. What can go wrong: a planned length that cuts a week in half, since Monday's customers can shop differently from Sunday's, so whole weeks are usually safer.

steps.title: Novelty: the lead that fades.
steps.text: A novelty effect is a change that does well because it is new, and fades as people get used to it. To see one, split the result by time in three steps. First, count each door's rate for week 1 alone. Second, for week 2 alone. Third, compare the leads. B got 72.3% in week 1 and 69.8% in week 2; A got 69.9% and 70.0%. B led in week 1 and was level with A, even a shade behind, in week 2. Day 4's 76.6% for B, the good day, fell in the first week. A test stopped in its first days measures the novelty, not the assistant. What can go wrong: two weeks may still be too short when customers visit monthly; then compare first-time visitors with returning ones, or run longer.

steps.title: Two kinds of feedback, and the guard rail that stops a door.
steps.text: Explicit feedback is what a customer tells you when asked: a thumbs up, a star rating. Implicit feedback is what they do: a refund, a return, the same question asked again a minute later, a chat abandoned. Fernhallow's dashboard showed only the explicit kind, and B's warmer, surer advice pleased people in the chat and failed them at the fitting. A guard-rail metric is a number the change is not meant to improve but must not make worse, watched with a line agreed before the start. It works in three steps: first, name it (refunds); second, set its line (3.5%, half a point above A's 3.00%); third, check it as the data arrive, and stop the variant when it crosses. Refunds arrive up to 7 days late, so the first check is day 8: B's day-1 refunds were 27 of 602, 4.49%, over the line. What can go wrong: one day is a small sample, so a real guard rail usually tests its gap too, and a line set too loose, such as 5.0%, never fires. Dead Letter Season 6, Night Shift Protocols, puts guard rails on releases in Canary in the Mine.

diagram.aria: The fix, replayed on the logged fortnight. The plan, written first: 8,077 chats a door, 14 days, one look, a refund line of 3.5%. Day 4's p of 0.018 is never read. On day 8 the guard rail sees B's day-1 refunds, 4.49%, over the line, and B stops. Had it run, day 14 gave p 0.116, no winner. Below, 200 A/A tests show why one look: checked daily, 43 find a false winner; checked once, 7.

explain.caption: Read left to right. The plan comes first: 8,077 chats a door, 14 days, one look, a refund line of 3.5%. Day 4's p of 0.018 is never read. On day 8, B's day-1 refunds are complete: 27 of 602, 4.49%, over the line, so B stops. Had it run, day 14 gave p 0.116 and no winner. Below: why one look, from 200 A/A tests: daily looks find 43 false winners, one look finds 7.

fix.title: The fix: plan the test before it starts, read it once, and let the refunds stop a door
fix.text: Before the first visitor: write down the main measure (the thumbs-up rate), the smallest gap worth catching, the sample size that follows (8,077 chats a door, 14 days, two whole weeks), and the one rule that decides (p below 0.05 on day 14). Name the guard-rail metrics with their lines: refunds above 3.5%, and, if you can count them, complaints and repeat questions. Let a coin pick each visitor's door and keep it. During the test, watch the guard rails as their data arrive and stop the variant if one crosses its line; leave the thumbs-up rate alone until the end. At the end, read the result once, split it by week, and read the refund notes. If the team truly needs to look early, plan a fixed number of looks and use a sequential test with a stricter line at each one.

limits: A guard rail on refunds is a week late by nature. B served 8 days and 4,796 chats before its line could fire; a faster signal, such as repeat questions about size, would help, if it tracks refunds.
One look at a fixed sample size is slower than stopping on a good day, and a real gap smaller than 2 points will often be missed. That is the price of believing the gaps you do find.

A coin and a fortnight still miss slow effects: a customer who returns boots in month two, or tires of the voice in month three. Some teams keep a small share on the old door for weeks after a release to check.

explain.seniorTake: An A/B test is the one evaluation that measures real customers, and it is easy to fool. Let a coin, not the customer, pick the door. Fix the sample size and the decision rule before the start, run whole weeks, and read the main measure once; every extra look is another chance for luck. Watch guard-rail metrics, the numbers that must not get worse, as their data arrive, with lines that stop a variant. Pair explicit feedback with implicit feedback, because what people say in the chat and what they do afterwards can point opposite ways. And split the result by week before trusting a lead that might be novelty.

realWorld.title: Evan Miller, 2010: How Not To Run an A/B Test
realWorld.text: Miller warns that stopping a test the moment it looks significant means you might be falling prey to what statisticians call repeated significance testing errors. His summary: if you peek at an ongoing experiment ten times, then what you think is 1% significance is actually just 5% significance. In his worst case, checking after every visitor on a change that does nothing, the false alarm rate he works out is 26.1%, more than five times the 5% the test claims.

realWorld.title: Miller's fix: decide first, then wait
realWorld.text: His advice is short: Decide on a sample size in advance and wait until the experiment is over. Looking is fine, he says, as long as you don't stop early on what you see, and he closes with no peeking!

realWorld.title: Microsoft's experimentation team on guardrail metrics
realWorld.text: Machmouchi, Gupta and Zhang of Microsoft's Experimentation Platform list guardrail metrics as the ones that measure aspects of the product that we don't want to degrade but won't necessarily improve. They recommend that a feature crew set up alerts for their business-critical metrics, naming guardrails such as page load time and error rates.

realWorld.title: Stopping a harmful test automatically
realWorld.text: The same article recommends setting up auto-shutdown for A/B tests that significantly degrade the product or the user experience, so issues are resolved as soon as they are detected instead of relying on (a possibly delayed) manual intervention. It reports such auto-shutdowns being used when a bug in a Bing A/B test led to a 404 page.

realWorld.title: Kohavi, Tang and Xu, 2020
realWorld.text: Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang and Ya Xu's book Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing is the standard text on running these tests at large companies, and, as we understand it, treats guardrail metrics as a class of their own beside the main measure. We could not fetch a primary excerpt, so read the book rather than our summary.

realWorld.title: The two-proportion z-test
realWorld.text: The test the sim works by hand is the usual one for comparing two shares: pool the successes, p = (x1 + x2) / (n1 + n2), and divide the gap between the two rates by the square root of p(1 - p)(1/n1 + 1/n2), and read the p-value from the normal curve. The pooled form is the one used for testing whether two shares are equal.

asked: How would you A/B test an LLM feature?
Why not stop a test as soon as it is significant?
interview.answer: Start offline: a golden set catches answers that are plainly wrong before any customer sees them. Then online. Assign users at random, with the assignment kept per user, so the two groups differ only in the variant. Choose one main measure, such as task success or thumbs up, and decide in advance the smallest gap worth catching, the false alarm rate and the power; that gives the sample size and the length, in whole weeks. Name guardrail metrics, the numbers that must not get worse, with stop lines: for an LLM feature, refunds or returns, complaints, repeat questions, escalations to a person, latency and cost. Watch those as data arrive and stop a variant that crosses a line; auto-shutdown is better than a person reading alerts. Do not stop on the main measure early. Each look gives luck another chance: Evan Miller showed that ten peeks turn a 1% test into a 5% one, and in our sim, daily checks on 200 A/A tests found 43 false winners against 7 with one look. If you must look early, plan the looks and use a sequential method. Pair explicit feedback, thumbs and ratings, with implicit feedback, what users do next, because a confident model can please in the chat and fail afterwards. Split by week and by new against returning users to catch novelty. Finally, read a sample of the conversations behind the numbers.

terms.def: Someone who counts what happened each day, overnight, so the numbers are ready by morning. Thandeka is Fernhallow's.
A program that writes text one likely word at a time, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown huge (a1e01). Fernhallow's shopping assistant is one.
A chat window on a shop's website, run by a language model, that answers questions and suggests what to buy. Fernhallow has two: A, the current one, and B, warmer and more confident.
The share of chats that end with a thumbs up (a5e01). At Fernhallow no tap counts as down, so it is thumbs up divided by all chats.
Splitting live visitors at random between two versions and comparing what happens with each (a5e01). Like two doors with a coin deciding which one you walk through.
One of the versions in an A/B test. Here, door A (the current assistant) and door B (the new one).
Letting chance, a computer's coin toss, decide each visitor's version, so the two groups are alike in everything except the version. If people chose, the keen would pick the new one.
Learning how a system behaves from real users after a change is live: ratings, refunds, A/B tests (a5e01). Offline evaluation checks prepared questions before.
A fixed list of real inputs with the right answers agreed in advance, used to score every version before it reaches users (a5e01).
How many chats each door needs, fixed before the start, to have a fair chance of catching a gap of a chosen size. Fernhallow's: 8,077 a door, 14 days.
The chance a test catches a real gap of the size you planned for. 80% is usual: one real 2-point rise in five would be missed.
A screen of numbers a team watches to see how something is doing. Fernhallow's showed both thumbs-up rates and the p-value, counted from day 1.
If the two versions were really the same, how often a gap at least this big would turn up by luck in a test read once. Not the chance that B is not better.
Here, a p-value below 0.05, a line chosen in advance: fewer than one time in twenty by luck. Its promise holds only for a test read once, at a fixed sample size.
Both doors' thumbs up over both doors' chats, as if they were one door. Days 1 to 4: 3,426 of 4,800, 71.4%.
The size of gap luck alone usually makes between two rates with this many chats. Day 4: 0.0130, about 1.3 points.
Written z: the gap between two rates divided by the standard error: how many luck-sized steps apart they are. Day 4: 2.36; day 14: 1.57.
The usual test for whether two shares, such as two thumbs-up rates, differ by more than luck: pool, find the standard error, divide the gap by it, read p from the normal curve.
The bell-shaped curve that gaps made by luck usually follow. About 95% of them fall within 1.96 standard errors of zero.
Reading a test's result before it has reached its sample size, and stopping if it looks good. Each look is another chance for luck to cross the line.
A version a test declares better when it isn't. Also called a false positive. Daily looks found 43 in 200 A/A tests; one look found 7.
An A/B test with the same version behind both doors, so any winner is luck. Used to check how often a test's rules cry wolf.
A test designed to be looked at several times, at planned points, with a stricter line at each look so the overall false alarm rate stays where you set it.
A change doing well because it is new, then fading as people get used to it. B's thumbs-up rate: 72.3% in week 1, 69.8% in week 2.
What users tell you when asked: a thumbs up or down, a star rating, a written comment.
What users do without being asked: a refund, a return, the same question asked again, a chat abandoned. Often slower to arrive, and harder to fake.
Money given back when a customer returns what they bought. At Fernhallow one arrives 2 to 7 days after the chat that led to the sale.
Refunds divided by chats. Over the fortnight: door A 252 of 8,407, 3.00%; door B 378 of 8,393, 4.50%.
A number a change isn't meant to improve but must not make worse, such as refunds or complaints, watched during a test with a line that stops a variant if crossed.
The limit agreed before a test for a guard-rail metric. Here, B's refund rate above 3.5% stops B; it fires on day 8, at 4.49%.
A guard rail that stops a variant by itself when it crosses its line, rather than waiting for a person to read an alert.
The one number a test is run to decide on, chosen in advance. Fernhallow's was the thumbs-up rate.
The moment a batch of changes goes live for every customer. Fernhallow releases every second Monday; B went to everyone on day 15.
Short for large language model: a language model trained on a very large amount of text.

atWork: Look for a feature at work that was chosen by an A/B test, and find the test's plan. A common pattern: a product team ships the variant that won in its first week, the dashboard was checked every morning, and the win was gone a month later, with a cost nobody was measuring. Ask five things. Was the sample size, and the day of the decision, written down before the test started, and did the test run to it? How many times was the result looked at before then? Did a coin decide each user's version, or did users choose? Which numbers were guard-rail metrics, with which lines, and how late does each one arrive: refunds and returns take days, complaints and escalations to a person take hours? And was the result split by week, or by new against returning users, to catch novelty? Dead Letter Season 6, Night Shift Protocols, covers guard rails on releases in Canary in the Mine.

recall.prompt: Your team is comparing two reply styles for a support chatbot in a three-week A/B test. On day 5 the dashboard shows the new style's rating ahead with p = 0.03, and your manager wants to switch everyone over tonight. What do you tell them, and what would you set up?

keyIdeas.idea: Stopping at the first p below 0.05 inflates false winners; run to the sample size fixed in advance
An early lead may be a novelty effect that fades
Watch guard-rail metrics with stop lines: numbers that must not get worse

recall.model: I'd say not tonight. Stopping at the first p below 0.05 is peeking: every morning's look gives luck another chance, so false winners turn up far more often than 1 in 20. I'd run to the end, the full three weeks, at the sample size fixed in advance, and read it once. Day 5 is also early enough for a novelty effect: people like a new style for a while and it can wear off, so I'd split the result by week. And I'd set up guard-rail metrics with stop lines, numbers that must not get worse, such as complaints, repeat questions and escalation to a person, checked as they arrive, so a style that pleases in the chat but fails afterwards is stopped.

recall.prompt: Two doors hold the same assistant, so any winner is luck. Read once at the end, about 1 in 20 such tests shows p below 0.05. In the sim's 200 such tests, checked every morning for 14 days and stopped at the first p below 0.05, how many found a winner?
recall.why: Each morning's look is another chance for luck to dip below 0.05, so 43 of 200 found a false winner, more than one in five. Read once on day 14, 7 of 200 did, close to the 1 in 20 the p-value promises. 10 of 200 is the promise itself, which only holds for one look.

recall.prompt: A product manager wants to put a banner on the site inviting customers to try the new assistant, then compare the thumbs-up rate of those who click with everyone else's. What is wrong with that, and what would you do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: People who choose the new version differ from those who don't, so the gap mixes people and assistant
Let a coin, random assignment, decide each user's version and keep it
Fix the sample size and decision rule in advance

recall.model: The customers who click are not like the rest: the keen and the curious self-select, so they'd rate any assistant differently. The gap would mix different people with a different assistant, and you couldn't tell which caused it. Instead, assign users at random, a coin per user, kept on every visit, so the two groups are alike except for the assistant. And fix the sample size and the decision rule in advance, then read the result once.

recall.prompt: Which of these is implicit feedback on a shopping assistant?
options: A thumbs down at the end of a chat
A star rating the customer was asked for
A refund, or the same question asked again a minute later
A written review on the product page
recall.why: Implicit feedback is what customers do without being asked: refunds, returns, repeat questions, abandoned chats. Thumbs, stars and reviews are explicit: the customer tells you. Fernhallow watched only the explicit kind, and B pleased in the chat while failing at the fitting.

recall.prompt: On the morning of day 5, counting days 1 to 4, the dashboard showed p = 0.018. Which reading is right?
options: There is a 1.8% chance that B is not really better than A
If the doors were the same, a gap this big would show by luck in about 1.8% of tests read once
B will keep its 3.1-point lead 98.2% of the time
The test has collected 98.2% of the chats it needs
recall.why: A p-value assumes no real difference and asks how often luck alone would make a gap this big, for a test read once at a fixed size. It is not the chance B is worse or better. Read every morning, it promised less: day 14 gave p = 0.116.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The written plan stuck. In March we tested C, an assistant that asks for the customer's usual boot size before suggesting one, against A: 8,100 chats a door, 14 days, one look, refund line 3.5%. C's refunds never came near the line: 3.1%, against A's 3.0%. On day 14, C had 72.6% thumbs up against A's 71.0%, a lead of 1.6 points, p = 0.023. Mr Coxwell wants to ship it. Then I split it by week: C led by 2.9 points in week 1 and by 0.3 in week 2.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Is C's win real, and what should happen before it ships?

keyIdeas.idea: Most of the lead is in the first week: likely a novelty effect fading
Check on later data: run longer, or compare new and returning visitors, before trusting the lead
The guard rail passed: refunds are not a reason to stop, so the question is only the main measure

coldCase.model: The rule was followed, so p = 0.023 is honest for what it measured. But nearly all of C's lead is in week 1, which looks like a novelty effect: people like the new voice and the shine wears off. A 0.3-point lead in week 2 may be nearly nothing. Before shipping, I'd check on later data: extend the test by two more weeks with a new plan for that question, written down first, or compare new visitors with returning ones, since a new visitor sees nothing new. The guard rail passed, and refunds at 3.1% are under the line, so they are not a reason to stop; the question is only whether the thumbs-up lead lasts. If it does, ship C, and keep a small holdout on A for a month.

sources.title: Evan Miller, How Not To Run an A/B Test, 18 April 2010, read 14 October 2026: repeated significance testing errors; if you peek at an ongoing experiment ten times, then what you think is 1% significance is actually just 5% significance; 26.1% in the worst case; Decide on a sample size in advance and wait until the experiment is over; no peeking

Widad Machmouchi, Somit Gupta and Ruhan Zhang, Microsoft Experimentation Platform, Patterns of Trustworthy Experimentation: During-Experiment Stage, 25 January 2021, read 14 October 2026: guardrail metrics measure aspects of the product that we don't want to degrade but won't necessarily improve; alerts on business-critical metrics; auto-shutdown for A/B tests that significantly degrade the product

Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang and Ya Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing, Cambridge University Press, 2020, book page read 14 October 2026 (no excerpt on guardrail metrics fetched)
Wikipedia, Two-proportion Z-test, read 14 October 2026: pooled proportion (x1 + x2) / (n1 + n2) and pooled standard error; pooled variance is appropriate for hypothesis testing of equality
